source.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
source.authors: Bilal Chughtai; Lawrence Chan; Neel Nanda

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares learned features and circuits across seeds, groups, and architectures, finding a shared algorithmic family but variation in which specific representations are learned. It therefore refines universality rather than testing convergence with scale or cross-modal alignment.
record.gate_note: The paper reports representation identities learned in Tables 5 and 6 separately by group, architecture, and seed; these are recorded individually below. It also reports other mechanistic results and cited findings, but they do not measure the claim versions catalogued here. No AI-directed instructions occur in the text.
record.test_reason: The study trains MLPs and Transformers on seven group-composition tasks over four seeds each. It reverse-engineers which group representations (features) and circuits every network learns. It finds a shared algorithm family, but the specific features vary by seed and architecture. Its own results therefore bear directly on whether the same features recur across seeds (V3) and models (V5), and on how complete convergence is (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find weak but not strong universality: all networks implement variants of the GCR algorithm, but networks with the same architecture learn different sets of representations, in different orders and numbers. Reverse-engineering a single network is therefore insufficient.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses mechanistic reverse engineering and group-theoretic feature identities across toy networks, rather than measuring cross-model distance alignment as models scale or comparing representations across paired modalities.
record.method_sensitivity: Learned representations and their order vary with random seed, group, and architecture; Transformers learn fewer representations than MLPs despite having more parameters.
record.problems: The study uses small models on synthetic group-composition tasks, not practical large models. Its cross-model comparison is based on identified representation sets rather than a direct representation-similarity measure; the authors explicitly leave applicability to larger practical models for future work.
record.rows_left_out: No per-seed key-representation lists from Tables 5 and 6 were omitted. Other reported measurements, including averaged FVE and loss statistics in Table 3, were left out because they characterize the algorithm's implementation or ablation performance rather than directly measuring recurrence of feature identities.

untested.parts: No comparison of alignment as model size or capability grows. Appendix C.1.1 gives only a qualitative note that hidden size (32-256) had no noticeable effect on which representations were learned.
No unit-level or basis-level similarity metric. Only the identity of the learned irreducible representations is compared.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation test.
No SAE features or practical large models. The authors leave larger models to future work.
No comparison of similarity measures or input distributions.
Whether shared data or objectives explain the alignment is not tested. Seeds share identical data and still diverge, which only indirectly bears on this part.

missing.what: Counts of how often each S5 representation is learned, and how many key representations are learned, over 50 MLP seeds. Sign and standard are most common; 6d is never learned.
Averaged FVE and ablation results showing the GCR algorithm is learned in every group and architecture. This is the weak-universality evidence.
Hidden size 32-256 had no noticeable effect on which representations were learned (qualitative only).
Transformers consistently learn fewer representations than MLPs despite having more parameters.

record.verdict_notes: Five MLP rows (R21, R25-R28) have values wrong or copied from Table 6; corrections are given above. A single per-seed row cannot by itself show convergence; the verdicts rest on comparing rows within each group and architecture. These are toy algorithmic tasks with known ground-truth features, so 'features' here means irreducible representations, not SAE features or neurons.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of representational alignment as model size or capability increases.
No paired image-caption or other vision-language comparison.
The study tests same-task networks across seeds, groups, and architectures, but does not compare individual units or learned bases using a similarity metric.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
The study tracks recurrence of group-theoretic representations as features, not recurrence of SAE features, neurons, or circuits in practical models.
No comparison of similarity measures, settings such as neighbour count, or input distributions.
The study finds incomplete consistency in which representations are learned, but does not test whether shared data or objectives, rather than a common model of reality, cause alignment.

source_check.correct: V3: absent concrete-feature recurrence; standard is absent from the other A5 Transformer seeds. V5: standard recurs in A5 MLPs, so the cross-architecture result differs.

relationships.condition: Cyclic and dihedral groups (C113, C118, D59, D61), MLP and Transformer, across seeds
relationships.reason: Every seed implements the same GCR circuit family, but the sets of key frequencies overlap only partly across seeds, and the learning order differs (R1-R16, R29-R44).
relationships.display_finding: Every seed implemented the GCR circuit family, but key-frequency sets overlapped only partly and learning order varied.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Cyclic and dihedral groups (C113, C118, D59, D61), MLP and Transformer, across seeds
source_check.reason: Valid as an overall qualification, but mixed condition groups require separate verdicts: C113 Transformer seeds 2 and 4 have no key representations shared with other seeds and warrant challenges for concrete-feature recurrence; other comparisons show incomplete overlap.

relationships.condition: Non-abelian groups S5, S6, A5, across seeds
relationships.reason: Recurrence is higher here: sign/standard recur in S5, and S6 Transformer seeds 2-4 are identical. Sets still differ across seeds, e.g. S6 Transformer seed 1 and A5 seed 4 (R17-R28, R45-R56). Figure 7's 50-seed S5 counts confirm this variation.
relationships.display_finding: Sign and standard representations recurred in S5, representation sets matched across S6 Transformer seeds 2–4 but differed in S6 Transformer seed 1 and A5 seed 4, and variation also appeared across 50 S5 seeds.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Non-abelian groups S5, S6, A5, across seeds
source_check.reason: The overall qualification is supported, but the condition group mixes strong recurrence with absence: A5 Transformer seed 4 shares no key representations with other A5 Transformer seeds and warrants a separate challenges verdict.

relationships.condition: Across MLP vs Transformer and seeds, all seven groups
relationships.reason: The same family of representation-theoretic features and circuits appears in every model (Table 3). Which specific features are used differs by model, and Transformers learn fewer representations than MLPs (R1-R56).
relationships.display_finding: Every model learned features and circuits from the same representation-theoretic family, but specific features varied and Transformers learned fewer representations than MLPs.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Across MLP vs Transformer and seeds, all seven groups
source_check.reason: Section 6 and Tables 3, 5–6 establish a recurring GCR algorithm family while specific representations and their number differ across models.

relationships.condition: Identical data, task and architecture, different seeds
relationships.reason: Convergence is incomplete even with identical training data: the specific features, their number and their order vary across seeds (R1-R56). The causal part of V7 is untested.
relationships.display_finding: Feature identities, number and ordering varied across seeds despite identical training data, task and architecture.

source_check.condition: Identical data, task and architecture, different seeds
source_check.reason: Section 6 explicitly reports different learned representations despite identical training data and architecture. This supports incomplete convergence only; plateauing and the proposed causal explanation remain untested.

relation.reason: Its own mechanistic analyses compare learned features and circuits across seeds and architectures.

tranche.reason: The study directly investigates universality and finds a shared algorithm family with variable concrete features, qualifying strong convergence claims.

source_check.notes: All 25 listed representation sequences match Tables 5–6 exactly. These are mechanistic feature identities, not a numerical alignment metric; the authors' weak-versus-strong universality conclusion is accurately paraphrased.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: same group and architecture, different seeds (Tables 5 and 6)
reader_labels.reason: The listed key-representation sets and their learning orders vary across initializations; the rows show both recurring representations and seed-specific selections (R1-R56).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: group-composition tasks across the tested seeds and architectures
reader_labels.reason: Some representations recur, but which representations are selected is not uniform across models (R1-R56); the paper characterizes the shared result as a family of circuits rather than identical features in every model.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: models trained for composition on the tested groups
reader_labels.reason: The feature sets vary between models despite the shared task; the results are consistent with partial rather than identical convergence. The causal role of shared data or objectives versus a common model of reality is not distinguished (R1-R56).
